speechtext: Mr. Speaker, the Secretary of State for External Affairs (Mr. Green) who has just given, as he said, his first formal statement in this kind of debate in that capacity, would not expect me to comment on all the topics that he has selected for his dissertation of today. He spoke of disarmament, NATO, the commonwealth, Canadian-United States relations, Latin America, Canada and the Pacific. Of course, when he was talking about Canada and the Pacific he neglected in his reply to the Leader of the Opposition (Mr. Pearson) to explain why in his present capacity he took a different view regarding Canadian participation in SEATO and particularly in ANZUS. The Secretary of State for External Affairs will remember that when he sat on this side of the house he strongly advocated that Canada should participate in these two international bodies operating in the Pacific.

speakerposition: Secretary of State for External Affairs
subtopic: EXTERNAL AFFAIRS
subsubtopic: REFERENCE OF ESTIMATES OF DEPARTMENT TO STANDING COMMITTEE
speechtext: I have learned a lot since then.

subtopic: EXTERNAL AFFAIRS
subsubtopic: REFERENCE OF ESTIMATES OF DEPARTMENT TO STANDING COMMITTEE
speechtext:
As my hon. friend said, he has learned a lot since then. I may say that if I do not agree with everything my hon. friend said he has expressed his views with a charm of manner which I must not allow to confuse me as I examine the substance of what he said.
He also spoke of the Middle East and then he mentioned, of course, the important work of the United Nations. I want to say at once to my hon. friend, with whom I have sat in this house since 1935, that notwithstanding our political differences I recognize, as all of

us in this house do-and I think this applies to the regard that each of us would have for one another-that the hon. gentleman is a sincere and honourable servant of the Canadian people. But in a matter of this kind and particularly, as the hon. gentleman has said, in view of the serious situations that confront the nations of the world, this is a time when we should devote ourselves thoughtfully and responsibly to the great issues that divide the two great divisions of the nations at this time.
I welcomed what the hon. gentleman had to say about disarmament. In view of the current discussion in Washington, in view of the fact that the disarmament commission is going to meet very shortly, in view of the difficulties attending the three power talks in Geneva at the moment, I should have thought, in the light of the minister's pronouncements outside this house regarding disarmament, that he would have taken the house into his confidence as to the Canadian proposals on disarmament, and given us some indication of the firm position of leadership and independence which the hon. gentleman thought Canada should pursue, not only on disarmament but in foreign affairs generally.
I agree with the Secretary of State for External Affairs that the evolution of this nation from colony to nation, from a country playing a limited part in foreign affairs to one where its position is recognized as important, is not now to be characterized merely as that of honest broker. I agree with what the Secretary of State for External Affairs has said in that regard, as indeed we were often reminded in this house by the Leader of the Opposition (Mr. Pearson) when, as secretary of state for external affairs he said repeatedly that not only should we seek to interpret the position of our friends to other countries, but that we should put forward positive positions reflecting our own national independence.
I am sure the minister did not wish to imply that in the immediate past, during the past 10 years, Canada had acted merely as an honest broker; for if there is anything that characterized the policies and the achievements of the Leader of the Opposition as secretary of state for external affairs it is that in association with the prime minister of that day the initiatives that he took did give Canada the reputation of exercising a responsible measure of independent judgment in some of the most vital matters affecting our generation.
It will not be forgotten that we played an independent role at Suez. It is very interesting to recall that Sir Anthony Eden referred,
External Affairs
in his book, to the balanced position which Canada took at that time and in that crisis. It will not be forgotten, I am sure, that the role that Canada played in respect of the troubles of old French Indo-China, following the Geneva accord of 1954, reflected the attitude not of a country that was merely an honest broker but of a country that recognized it had a role to play and a role she was determined to play in her relations with all countries, including her friendliest neighbours and associates, the United States and the United Kingdom.
It will not be forgotten that the role Canada played in the partition of Palestine was that of a country exercising an independent point of view and, likewise, our role in the Korean armistice discussions; our role in urging, in the North Atlantic Treaty Organization, that there should be collective economic action as well as collective political action in the interests of maintaining the defence of the western nations. Therefore, I think if the hon. gentleman refers now with pride, as he must and as he does and should, to the role Canada now pursues he will recognize that the foundations for that were laid in a brilliant manner by the hon. gentleman who sits immediately to my left.
The hon. gentleman spoke of South Africa and I am sure that any responsible member of this house will agree with him that any effort to exclude one commonwealth country from the commonwealth is a course that is not to be encouraged or supported. But that issue did not arise, and I do not say that the hon. gentleman said it did arise, in this house. That was a suggestion made outside this house; but I think, having in mind the well-known views that my hon. friend has and that his Prime Minister (Mr. Diefenbaker) has about the rights of man, one may properly urge in a debate of this sort that there would be nothing in violation of Article II, subsection 7, of the United Nations charter, if a responsible Canadian spokesman were to have declared a view that would be along the lines of those uttered by the prime minister of the United Kingdom when he spoke in South Africa the other day.
Speaking for myself, I say the courage and the statesmanship of those declarations made by the queen's first minister in the United Kingdom indicate that what Britain was able to do in respect of so delicate a matter, and on South African soil, is the kind of thing that one of the queen's first ministers in one of the commonwealth countries should not hesitate likewise to do in the interests of all that is involved. This does not in any way suggest that there is any desire on the part of anyone proposing such a declaration that he wants to see any dismemberment, or any

External Affairs
withdrawal from the commonwealth of any one of its constituents. I believe that if there is one thing that friends can do it is to talk frankly, and that is exactly what the prime minister of the United Kingdom did the other day in South Africa.
At first the hon. gentleman spoke of disarmament, and because I regard this as the current important question, as the question in respect of which Canada can make some contribution, I should like to give my views on this great problem. May I say that in opening what I have to say on disarmament I regret that the minister today, in talking about disarmament, did little more than acknowledge what I am sure we all recognize, namely the great importance to the world at this time of finding a solution to this problem, and particularly to the problem of nuclear disarmament.
As the hon. gentleman said, there is nothing that is more dangerous in our time than the competitive position of great instruments of war capable of destroying not only the armies and the civilian populations of the world but even, as he said, possibly civilization itself. If that is the case, as it is, then certainly a country that has been designated as one of the members of the 10-power committee on disarmament owes to this parliament a greater demonstration of interest than merely to affirm the importance of disarmament in relation to the peace of the world.
There is a meeting of the western countries on the disarmament committee under way now in Washington. The minister pointed out that Canada is a member of the 10-power committee designated by the foreign ministers last September, note of which was taken by the United Nations at the general assembly, and that our representative on that body is a former distinguished public servant and soldier of Canada. I should have thought that if the minister and the government thought that disarmament was so important we would have had outlined today the proposals that Canada has in mind. It cannot be argued that the proposals for disarmament which Canada may have are necessarily fully secret. After all, Great Britain put forward a proposal in the United Nations through her foreign minister last September and chairman Khrushchev of the Soviet union, speaking from the rostrum of the United Nations, outlined the soviet's proposal. The other day we were given a precis of the French position which we are told Mr. Jules Moch of France is taking in the current meetings in Washington.
In any event, it would seem to me that Canada's parliament should have an opportunity of knowing not only the principles- admittedly these are important-that Canada
[Mr. Martin (Essex East) .1
has in mind in approaching this problem, but that likewise, we should have some idea of the position that Canada is going to take on disarmament. Whether or not Canada has a proposal I do not know but if Canada has a proposal it seems to me that the house might well ask the minister to indicate that proposal so that we can debate this matter properly and see whether or not the independent position in international affairs of which the hon. gentleman spoke is going to be maintained.
For instance, I asked the minister a question yesterday and the minister did not reply. As I explained to him privately today I would have given him notice of that question but it was a supplementary question. I thought that possibly he would have simply suggested in reply that he would like to take the question as notice. The gist of my question had to do with the reply that he made yesterday when he said that Canada took the position that there should be a ban on nuclear tests. I am not now quarrelling with that position. But the minister having taken that position I would ask him if he does not think that the Canadian position in that particular should be made known to Canada's colleagues, particularly the western colleagues, three countries on the 10-power committee.

speakerposition: Secretary of State for External Affairs
subtopic: EXTERNAL AFFAIRS
subsubtopic: REFERENCE OF ESTIMATES OF DEPARTMENT TO STANDING COMMITTEE
speechtext: They already know that.

subtopic: EXTERNAL AFFAIRS
subsubtopic: REFERENCE OF ESTIMATES OF DEPARTMENT TO STANDING COMMITTEE
speechtext:
My hon. friend says that they already know that. Perhaps in order to give precision to my question I might read it so that we will be clear about what we are seeking to establish. I asked the minister the following question which will be found at page 866 of Hansard:
I should like to ask the Secretary of State for External Affairs a supplementary question arising out of his statement just a moment ago that the position of the government was that it was against nuclear tests without any reservation. I should like to ask him if this decision has been made known to the western powers with which Canada is now conferring in Washington prior to meetings of the disarmament commission-
The minister now says that the Canadian position is known to our western colleagues on the committee. Then I went on to ask if Canada had been informed by the United States and Great Britain or by each of them separately of positions which it is widely reported they are going to take before the end of the week at the conference now under way between the three nuclear powers in Geneva. I think the answer to that question has very great significance because while there has been agreement on 20 articles of the proposed treaty in the discussions now current in Geneva they have reached a critical position with regard to the question of controls beyond the threshold in respect of the detonation of nuclear weapons underground. The situation that could flow from

the position which my hon. friend took yesterday is that we might And ourselves in relation to the Soviet union, assuming that they were not insistent on controls at that particular point, taking the same position which that country takes and finding ourselves opposed to the position which the United Kingdom and the United States might be taking in a matter where apparently they may continue to insist on controls even at what is called the threshold level.
My hon. friend will see that the independent position about which he spoke a while ago is one which I readily admit should unhesitatingly be asserted but it is one that, if taken, should be explained in relation to specific issues such as the one to which I have just referred. This great emphasis on disarmament at the present time has been focussed largely at this period, I think, as a result of the proposal made by chairman Khrushchev on September 14 last at the United Nations-

speakerposition: Secretary of State for External Affairs
subtopic: EXTERNAL AFFAIRS
subsubtopic: REFERENCE OF ESTIMATES OF DEPARTMENT TO STANDING COMMITTEE
speechtext: And Mr. Lloyd.

subtopic: EXTERNAL AFFAIRS
subsubtopic: REFERENCE OF ESTIMATES OF DEPARTMENT TO STANDING COMMITTEE
speechtext:
And as a result of the statement later made by the secretary of state for foreign affairs in the United Kingdom, Mr. Selwyn Lloyd, to whom I referred a moment ago and whose proposal is in the detailed form which I have argued in the house during the past few minutes, should characterize the attitude of the government in this. If Great Britain can put forward a detailed proposal on disarmament, so can Canada whose responsibilities in this matter as a member of the 10-power committee are no less important.
The Leader of the Opposition expressed the viewpoint, I think, of those of us on this side of the house and the people of Canada generally when, in referring to the Khrushchev proposal, he said on September 22, 1959, speaking to the Women's Canadian Club of Vancouver:
Perhaps the proposal has already served its purpose, it it is mere propaganda, because the west reaction to it has been uncertain and delayed. Would it not have been wise for the western governments, especially that ot the United States, to have responded at once, very simply but very definitely and effectively? Could our leaders not have said right after the proposal was made: "Total disarmament, admirable, that is our policy. We accept your proposal on the assumption, of course, that at the end of the four year period"-
That was the prescribed period put forward by the head of the government of the Soviet union.
-we will have not only a treaty for disarmament but one for international inspection and control without which a disarmament treaty would be a mockery.
I think we all recognize that that statement is one that contains a great deal of
External Affairs
wise direction and I agree at once with what the Secretary of State for External Affairs himself said at the assembly last January, that this proposal ought to be taken as a serious proposal put forward by one of the five great powers and that every effort ought to be made to test its sincerity, its validity and its acceptability. We may have our reservations, we may have our views as to why the proposal was made. We will want to test it in the light of the kind of controls the west properly now insists must exist. But in our desire to try to bring about the achievement of full or partial disarmament, I agree that our approach to this matter must be objective and as free from sinister or needlessly provocative language as possible.
Something obviously must be done about this problem of the race in armaments. 1 came across some very interesting observations of Mr. Winston Churchill on the matter of the hideous race for armaments. One statement was made in the British parliament before the first world war in 1912 and the other, in the same vein, was pronounced in the house of commons of the United Kingdom prior to the second world war. Mr. Churchill said in 1912:
I cannot believe that after armaments of all countries have reached a towering height, they will settle down and continue at a hideous level far above the present level-already crushing- and that that will be for many years a normal feature of the world routine.
Then, in 1936, referring to these same words which I have just quoted, he said:
Whatever happens I do not believe that. Europe is approaching a climax. I believe that climax will be reached during the lifetime of the present parliament. Either there will be a melting of hearts, and a joining of hands between great nations -which will set out to realize the glorious age of prosperity now within the reach of millions of toiling people-or there will be an explosion and a catastrophe, the course of which no imagination can measure and no human eye can see.
The second world war allowed and now we are faced with the implications of these two statements, only in regard to a situation that is certainly more cataclysmic in its potential than the situation which prevailed before the two world wars. In this matter, Canada, just as much as the United States and Great Britain or any of the great powers, has a responsibility to give leadership-even if that involves taking responsible issue with those friends with whom we are ever dedicated in the prosecution of a common purpose-in pursuit of the desire to maintain peace in the world. This is undoubtedly what the hon. gentleman himself had in mind when, speaking in the general assembly on September 24, 1959, he said:
The middle-sized and smaller powers must have an opportunity of being heard, for disarmament is

External Affairs
of the deepest concern to all mankind. In Canada's work on the committee, we shall at all times keep these considerations very much in mind.
I applaud those words of the minister. Every member of this house will applaud those words of the minister, as will the people of Canada. However, they will expect those words to be translated into courageous, responsible and honourable action as a member of the 10-power committee. My hon. friend will perhaps permit me to say, and I must say frankly, that I admire the sincerity of the hon. gentleman in this matter of disarmament. I admire the general declarations he has made. We all support them. However, the test of the hon. gentleman's contribution will come within the course of the next few months when we shall see to what extent Canada, as a member of the 10-power committee, is prepared to take a strong position, not only against the Soviet union if necessary, but against any other power no matter how friendly, who seems at the moment to be pursuing a course not calculated to further the advancement of disarmament.
I know that the hon. gentleman, his government and that distinguished soldier General Burns will approach this matter on the basis of the fact that since the end of the second world war we have all recognized that disarmament can only be achieved on a multilateral basis; that the concepts which existed before the two wars can no longer prevail. Unilateral disarmament is not desirable, indeed it is dangerous. We must insist upon adequate safeguards and controls, as I hope to show later in more detail when I discuss what I believe our specific attitude should be at this time. I would simply say we have always, in the west, maintained it was necessary to have a system of controls. We had to take mutually those measures which would guarantee to each state the implementation by the others of a solemn undertaking made with regard to partial or full disarmament.
We have had trouble with the Soviet union in this particular. They have not been forthcoming with our requests for the kind of controls which we envisage as necessary. It is perhaps interesting historically to recall that in 1816 Alexander I of Russia proposed to Castlereagh that there should be a reduction in the armed forces of Europe. The interesting fact is that at that time the only European country that was on a real war footing was Russia. Then, Metternich, when he replied to Castlereagh, commented upon this proposal of Alexander's and said that his reaction was that because of the difficulties always in obtaining any true data from Russia, to take the initiative here, uncertain of a reciprocity of confidence, would be impossible. I do not say that history is always germane but I do say, as one who had some modest participation in some of the disarmament discussions, that one of the main reasons for the failure of the 12 frustrating years was the reluctance of the Soviet union to satisfy the west in the matter of controls. I do not say the whole blame rests on the shoulders of the Soviet union.
Perhaps, Mr. Speaker, you will allow me to adjourn the debate and deal with this question when I resume tomorrow.
On motion of Mr. Martin (Essex East) the debate was adjourned.
